Tuning Sourdough Hydration

By Ada Baker

Hydration is the ratio of water to flour in a dough, expressed as a percentage of the flour weight. A dough with 1000 grams of flour and 750 grams of water sits at seventy-five percent hydration, which is a comfortable middle ground for most home bakers working with a levain and a mix of bread flour and whole wheat.

Why hydration matters

Higher hydration produces a more open crumb and a thinner, crackly crust, but it also makes the dough stickier and harder to shape. Lower hydration gives a tighter crumb that is easier to slice for sandwiches. The flour guide explains how protein content changes how much water a flour can absorb before the dough turns slack.

Adjusting for whole grain flour

Whole wheat and rye flours absorb noticeably more water than white flour because bran and germ soak up moisture slowly. When you swap twenty percent of the white flour for whole wheat, add roughly five percent more water and give the dough an extra thirty minutes of autolyse so the bran can hydrate fully. See the autolyse entry and the levain notes.

Reading the dough during bulk fermentation

Temperature changes everything during bulk fermentation. A warm kitchen speeds fermentation and makes a high hydration dough feel looser, so shorten the bulk and add an extra set of coil folds to build strength. In a cold kitchen the same dough may need several more hours before it is airy, domed and jiggly.

def hydration(water_g, flour_g):
    return round(100 * water_g / flour_g, 1)
StyleHydration
Sandwich loaf65%
Country loaf75%
Open crumb85%

Quick checklist

  • Weigh flour and water, never use cups.
  • Hold back ten percent of the water and add it during mixing.
  • Note the kitchen temperature next to every bake.
